column1: # ---- 04-compliance/T4 ----
The fill model is FillProbView's underlying probability-of-fill surface and the derived reliable-volume bounds that cross C1, and it is a prediction about an external system.

The quoting policy is the mapping from target, shadow value, urgency, fill curve and microstructure state to a limit-order ladder, and it is a policy whose quality is measured rather than a function whose correctness is asserted.
Neither the fill model nor the quoting policy has an invariant saying it must be true; both have a measured distance to reality and a band outside which that distance is a release blocker.
T4 is the only level whose output is a report rather than a pass/fail on a predicate, but the band is a gate and the gate is enforced.
The fill model's job is to predict the simulator's behaviour and its accuracy target is defined by that rather than by the real market in the abstract.
Predicting the simulator is a much narrower and more tractable problem than a general limit-order-book model, which is precisely why the fill-fidelity decision can remain deferred.
Whatever is calibrated against the simulator inherits the simulator's biases, and when the engine is pointed at a real venue the fill model must be recalibrated with the gap becoming a named risk.
Every T4 report carries a banner naming the calibration target simulator version, the simulator's version is part of the run manifest, and a calibration report that does not name its target is void.

A fill model artefact is stamped with the simulator version it was fitted against, and loading a fill model whose target version does not match the configured Execution adapter is a HALT at startup rather than a warning.
Measured accuracy against the simulator is not evidence of accuracy against a venue, and no document, dashboard or release note may present it as such.
The go-live gate requires a recalibration plan and a shadow period precisely because the simulator-measured accuracy number does not transfer.

Everything downstream that consumes fill quality — the executionSlippage bucket, the reliable-volume bounds and the quoting policy's capture ratio — inherits the simulator caveat and carries it in its own reporting.
When the simulator changes the fill model is re-verified before the release that consumes the new simulator rather than after.

The characterisation run is a designed grid sweep rather than a backtest of the strategy, so the calibration is not confounded by the strategy's own order placement which concentrates orders in a narrow region and leaves the rest of the surface unmeasured.
The price-band factor sweeps distance from the reference price in ticks or spread units from −3σ to +3σ relative to the intraday reference, signed by side.
The product factor covers each intraday product traded — quarter-hour, hour and block — per liquidity class.
The time-to-gate factor sweeps seven bands from more than eight hours down to under fifteen minutes.
Buy and sell are measured separately because the asymmetry is real and must not be averaged away.
The volume-bucket factor is small, typical and large relative to the product's observed depth, and the regime factor is ordinary, high-volatility, negative-price and high-imbalance.
Every cell must have a minimum observation count before it is reported, and cells below it are reported as insufficient data and are not interpolated over.
An interpolated cell that later turns out to be systematically wrong is indistinguishable from a measured one, which is the failure the no-interpolation rule prevents.
The characterisation run is a manifest-pinned run, so a calibration can be reproduced exactly and a re-calibration can be diffed against its predecessor.
Per-cell bias is realised minus predicted fill rate and must lie within plus or minus 0.05 for cells with at least 200 observations.
Aggregate bias is the volume-weighted mean bias across cells and must lie within plus or minus 0.02.
The Brier score is the mean squared error of the predicted fill probability and must not regress by more than 10 per cent against the previous calibration.
Log loss is reported under the same regression rule as the Brier score.
Fill rate is non-decreasing as the limit price becomes more aggressive within a cell family, and a violation with at least 200 observations on both sides blocks release.
Fill rate is non-decreasing as time-to-gate grows, all else equal, under the same treatment as price monotonicity.
The monotonicity relations are metamorphic relations on the fill model itself and are the cheapest defence against a mis-specified surface.
A fill model that predicts a lower fill probability for a more aggressive price has a sign error somewhere, and no amount of aggregate Brier score will reveal it.
A reliability diagram bins orders by predicted fill probability into deciles per product and time-to-gate band and plots realised frequency against predicted probability.
The reliability report carries the expected calibration error, the maximum calibration error, and the slope and intercept of the fitted reliability line.
Points on the diagonal mean the model is calibrated and no action is needed.

A reliability slope below one, with the curve flatter than the diagonal, means the model is over-confident and over-predicts extremes in both directions, and the fix is isotonic or Platt recalibration on a holdout rather than a global shrink of the surface.

A systematic offset above the diagonal means the model under-predicts fill and the Planner is leaving executable volume on the table via over-tight reliable-volume bounds, and the bias is conservative and therefore safe to ship pending the fix.

A systematic offset below the diagonal means the model over-predicts fill and the Planner is planning on volume it will not get, and this blocks release because it produces plans that are infeasible in practice.
A high maximum calibration error in one time-to-gate band only means the urgency dimension is mis-specified, and the check is whether the quoting policy's urgency input is on the same scale.

The asymmetry between the two offset directions is deliberate and mirrors the degradation philosophy: a conservative error costs revenue and is visible while an optimistic error costs feasibility and is not.

The same calibration machinery applies to the aFRR activation model, because the activation beliefs drive the SOC chance constraint and a mis-calibrated activation belief produces exactly the delivery shortfall treated as a prequalification risk.
Realised activation fraction versus predicted, by block, direction and regime, must have aggregate bias within plus or minus 0.03.
The activation reliability diagram carries the same asymmetry, with under-predicting activation the unsafe direction.

The realised frequency of SOC leaving the band must be at most the configured ε over the holdout, and a realised frequency above ε means the chance constraint is not delivering its stated confidence and blocks release.
The correlation between activation and price regime that the joint ensemble exists to preserve must be present in the realised data too, or the ensemble is mis-specified.

The chance-constraint calibration row is the one most often skipped and the one that matters, because ε is a promise about how often SOC feasibility is allowed to fail and an uncalibrated activation model makes that promise vacuous.
Calibration decays as the simulator, the products or the market regime change.
A rolling 20-day aggregate bias above 0.03 in magnitude warns, and above 0.05 alerts and raises a calibration ticket.
A rolling 20-day expected calibration error per product above 1.5 times its value at last calibration alerts.
A Page–Hinkley or CUSUM change point on the per-order calibration residual alerts continuously and names the day the drift started.
A previously-populated cell that is now insufficient data warns, because the strategy has stopped exploring a region and the surface is going stale there.
A simulator version hash differing from the fill model's stamped target is a HALT at startup.
Any new monotonicity violation with at least 200 observations alerts on the nightly run.
Drift alerts route to the calibration owner rather than to the on-call engineer, a calibration ticket has a due date measured in days, and a HALT does not.

Calibration drift is recorded in the settlement artefact so P&L can be conditioned on it, because a quarter in which the fill model drifted for three weeks should be attributable to that rather than to strategy.
The quoting policy is the component separated from the Planner precisely so its contribution to P&L is separately measurable.
The region between the prevailing market and the shadow value is the space the quoting policy is free to work in, and its job is to capture as much of it as fill probability allows.
For a sell fill the available spread is the reference market price minus the shadow value and the captured amount is the fill price minus the shadow value.
For a buy fill the available spread is the shadow value minus the reference market price and the captured amount is the shadow value minus the fill price.
The capture ratio is the volume-weighted sum of captured over the volume-weighted sum of available.
CommitmentCover legitimately captures poorly because it is buying certainty, and must not drag the headline capture ratio.
Capture should fall monotonically as urgency rises, and if it does not then urgency is not wired into the ladder.
Unfilled opportunity cost is the sum over unfilled intents of volume times available spread.

Capture ratio measured only on fills is the classic trap, because a policy that quotes at the shadow value captures zero per cent and fills nothing while a policy that quotes at the market captures one hundred per cent of nothing, so both must be in the same report.
The frontier view plotting capture ratio against fill rate per policy configuration is the useful one, and configurations are compared on the frontier rather than on either axis alone.
A fill that occurs precisely because the market was about to move against you is worth less than its price suggests, and adverse selection is the difference.
Adverse selection is the single most common way an execution policy that looks good on capture ratio loses money.
The markout of a fill at horizon Δ is the signed difference between the reference price at Δ after the fill and the fill price times volume, positive when the market moved in our favour.
Markout horizons are one minute, five minutes, fifteen minutes and to the gate.
A consistently negative markout means the policy is being picked off.

A markout decay curve that worsens monotonically with horizon indicates information-driven adverse selection, while one that recovers indicates transient impact, which is a different and less alarming problem.
Aggressive fills that crossed the spread should show near-zero markout by construction, and a negative markout on aggressive fills means the reference price itself is stale.
Capture net of adverse selection, in EUR, is the number that matters, because a policy with a high capture ratio and worse adverse selection is destroying value.
A quoting policy change ships only if capture net of adverse selection improves, or is neutral with a stated reason.
T4 asserts that the adverse-selection measurement and the executionSlippage bucket are consistent over the same period within tolerance.
A divergence between adverse selection and executionSlippage means one of the two definitions has drifted, and that divergence is exactly what the unexplained ratio starts registering months later.
The ex-ante trade-through check runs over every emitted intent every tick in production and in backtest, blocking an untagged violation and recording the magnitude.
The ex-post trade-through check runs over every fill from C4 reconciled against the recorded intent, recording the value destroyed as the price gap times volume.

The aggregate trade-through report carries the trade-through rate, the tagged rate, the untagged blocked count as the complement, the value destroyed in EUR, and cuts by tag, urgency decile and product.
An untagged trade-through that reached C3 is a stop-ship, because the enforcement point is broken rather than the policy.

A tagged CommitmentCover trade-through warns and is counted, is expected in small numbers, and a rising rate means commitments are being taken that the engine cannot cover economically — a reserve-sizing question rather than a quoting question.

Value destroyed above the configured budget over a period alerts and prompts review of the shadow value extraction itself, because a systematically wrong dual is a Planner defect surfacing as an execution symptom.
Trade-through concentrated in the top urgency decile warns, because the policy is panicking near the gate and the urgency mapping is too aggressive.
A high trade-through rate is more often a signal that the shadow value is being extracted incorrectly — an approximated dual rather than the real one — than that the quoting policy is misbehaving.
The shadow value on the position accounting constraint must be finite and its sign must be consistent with the position's direction.
Scaling all prices by k greater than zero scales the shadow value by k.
Both A/B arms consume the identical recorded PlanResult stream so the Planner is genuinely held fixed, which is only possible because PlanResult is recorded.
Both A/B arms use the same simulator version and manifest, because otherwise the comparison measures the simulator.
The A/B comparison is paired per tick and per product on the same instance, because a paired test has far more power than two independent backtests.
The A/B primary metric is capture net of adverse selection in EUR, volume-weighted.
The A/B guardrail metrics are trade-through rate, unfilled opportunity cost and CommitmentCover fill rate, because a policy that improves capture by failing to cover commitments has not improved.
The A/B result is reported with the simulator banner because it is a statement about the simulator.
Fill-rate calibration by price band determines whether the fill-probability BoundTerm is a scalar volume cap or a per-price-band cap, and the C2 contract shape does not change either way.
A conservative fill-rate bias is tightened toward truth while an optimistic bias is corrected immediately.
An under-confident activation model widens ε until recalibrated.
The reliability diagram slope feeds an isotonic recalibration layer on the fill model artefact, versioned and content-hashed like any other artefact.
Adverse selection by urgency feeds the quoting policy's urgency mapping.
Trade-through concentration feeds shadow-value extraction in the Planner.
Every drift alert feeds the mode transitions and the settlement record so P&L can be conditioned on the calibration state of the period.
A recalibrated fill model is a new artefact with a new hash, which makes it a new manifest, which makes every golden hash downstream of it change.
A recalibration is a deliberate behaviour change and should be visible as one, and the baseline update carries the calibration report as its justification.
One T4 report is produced per nightly run and one per release, both archived with the manifest.
The T4 report carries the manifest id, the calibration target simulator version, the window, and the order and fill counts.

The T4 report's fill model section carries aggregate bias against its band, the Brier score against the previous value, expected calibration error by product, monotonicity violations, insufficient cells, and the attached reliability diagrams per product and time-to-gate band.
The T4 report's activation model section carries aggregate bias against its band and the realised SOC-band exit frequency against epsilon.

The T4 report's quoting policy section carries the capture ratio by tag, urgency and time-to-gate, unfilled opportunity cost, adverse selection at each markout horizon, capture net of adverse selection as the primary metric, the trade-through rates, and the value destroyed.
The T4 report's drift section carries the Page–Hinkley change point, the rolling 20-day bias, and the open calibration tickets.
The T4 report closes with the caveat that every number in it is measured against the simulator and does not transfer to a live venue without recalibration.
A release proceeds when every pass/fail line passes, the primary quoting metric has not regressed, and any warning has an owner and a date.
